reviewType: AI-assisted source reading; not external theological approval
rule: Summaries are editorial paraphrases of each named author. Shared subject tags express relevance, not agreement. Comparison records link distinct positions without manufacturing a consensus or a historical exchange between authors.

treatments.locator: Comment on verse 7, from And thy seed after thee through To be a God unto thee; excludes translator footnotes
treatments.summary: Calvin includes Abraham's natural descendants in an outward covenant adoption while distinguishing those who effectually receive the promise through faith. He calls the covenant spiritual and directed to eternal salvation, with the land an added benefit.
treatments.limit: Does not imply every outward member is saved. No baptism conclusion is attributed solely from this selected paragraph.

treatments.locator: All verse-7 commentary paragraphs, especially the two applications of to be a God
treatments.summary: Gill distinguishes temporal and providential blessings for natural descendants from enduring grace and glory for spiritual descendants. The circumcision covenant's natural-seed administration reaches its fulfillment and end in Messiah, while the spiritual blessings endure.
treatments.limit: Do not reduce this to denial of all spiritual Abrahamic promises or label it as a direct reply to Calvin.

treatments.locator: Comments on verses 16-17: former afflictions, return from Babylon, and new heavens and earth
treatments.summary: Calvin begins the restoration with return from Babylon and extends its fulfillment through Christ's whole reign to the last resurrection. The new-world language describes church restoration, yet he also expects heaven and earth to be fully renewed with perfected humanity.
treatments.limit: Calling the language metaphorical must not erase his explicit final cosmic renewal.

treatments.locator: Opening commentary paragraph on new heavens and a new earth
treatments.summary: Gill traces an initial gospel-era fulfillment, a further fulfillment in the conversion of the Jews, and completion in the New Jerusalem with literal new heavens and earth.
treatments.limit: This passage alone does not establish a full millennial chronology; retain his stated stages without importing a system label.

treatments.locator: Author comments on Hebrews 8:7-13, especially verse 10 and his question about grace under the Law
treatments.summary: Calvin explains the new covenant through forgiveness, inward renewal and knowledge of God. He preserves saving grace among the Old Testament fathers while contrasting the relative administrations before and after Christ.
treatments.limit: Translator's notes and alternative renderings remain separate. Jeremiah is a supporting source within Hebrews; the entire Jeremiah passage is not automatically assigned exposition coverage.

treatments.locator: Comments on verses 6-12, especially verses 9 and 11; excludes notes marked Ed. and fj
treatments.summary: Calvin reads sanctuary access and the high priest's blood offering as patterns fulfilled in Christ. He identifies the greater tabernacle with Christ's body and distinguishes recurring animal offerings from Christ's effective, enduring redemption.
treatments.limit: Temple tag includes sanctuary/tabernacle treatment. The electronic editor corrects a Jeremiah cross-reference; that correction is not Calvin's wording.

treatments.locator: Comments on the shadow/image contrast and repeated sacrifices in Hebrews 10:1-4
treatments.summary: Calvin treats legal sacrifices as an incomplete portrayal of the same Christ and salvation, unable in themselves to settle guilt. Repetition supports his argument for the sufficiency of Christ's sacrifice.
treatments.limit: The source includes sixteenth-century anti-Roman polemic. It is preserved at source, not silently adopted as the project's editorial voice.

treatments.locator: Chapter IX, printed pp. 140-142; PDF pp. 150-152, including Peter's confession and church announcement
treatments.summary: Vos locates the church announcement in the historical moment of Peter's confession amid others' rejection. He emphasizes Peter as the steadfast confessor rather than treating the saying as detached from Jesus' ministry.
treatments.limit: Only this opening passage treatment has been assessed; the full chapter's ecclesiology has not been independently reviewed.

treatments.locator: Prolegomena, Leading Principles; 1915 scan printed pp. 12-13, PDF pp. 16-17
treatments.summary: Berkhof states his assumptions about inspiration, Scripture's own claims, early testimony and the limited use of working hypotheses. These are his stated interpretive commitments, not neutral premises attributed to all scholarship.
treatments.limit: A methodological section, not verse-level exposition or a substitute for the separate hermeneutics textbook.

comparisons.question: How does the covenant promise apply to Abraham's natural and spiritual descendants?
comparisons.sharedGround: Both distinguish natural descent from effectual spiritual participation.
comparisons.difference: Calvin describes a spiritual covenant outwardly offered to the natural seed, with salvation effectually received by faith. Gill assigns temporal providential benefits to the natural seed as such and enduring saving benefits to the spiritual seed.
comparisons.limits: Comparison is editorial and passage-specific. Neither automatic salvation by descent nor a complete baptism argument is inferred. No historical exchange between these authors is alleged.

comparisons.question: How do historical restoration, gospel renewal and final new creation relate?
comparisons.sharedGround: Both include gospel renewal and final renewal rather than limiting the passage to one immediate historical event.
comparisons.difference: Calvin starts from the return from Babylon and follows Christ's reign to the resurrection. Gill explicitly adds a future Jewish conversion stage between initial gospel fulfillment and the New Jerusalem.
comparisons.limits: This is not a simplistic metaphor-versus-literal opposition: Calvin also affirms final renewal of heaven and earth. Absence of a stage in this paragraph does not establish denial elsewhere.
